floors.content: What is a line? A stick dragged through wet sand leaves a straight groove. In general terms, that groove can be called a line.
Railway lines, phone lines, and help lines all use the same word in different ways. Underneath them is the idea of a path from one place to another.
In mathematics, a line is a straight one-dimensional figure with no thickness, extending infinitely in both directions.
A groove in sand, a railway track, and a laser beam may look like lines, but each one eventually stops somewhere.
A Euclidean line does not stop. It continues without an endpoint in both directions, beyond anything that can be physically drawn.
A true mathematical line is not found as an object in the world. It is an ideal concept: perfectly straight, infinitely long, and useful because of that perfection.
A railway track is not a true mathematical line. It is closer to a line segment: a straight piece with a start, an end, and a measurable length.
A ray has one starting point and then continues in one direction without an endpoint. It has a beginning, but no finishing point.
A segment has two endpoints, a ray has one endpoint, and a true line has no endpoints. The difference is the number of ends.
A blank line is not very informative on its own. Once evenly spaced marks are placed on it, the line can begin to carry numbers.
The first important mark is zero. It acts as the anchor point, giving every other number a position relative to the starting place.
Moving right from zero gives 1, 2, 3, and the rest of the counting numbers. Since the line keeps going, the counting can keep going too.
A true line extends in both directions, so the number line cannot stop at zero or only grow to the right.
Numbers to the left of zero are negative numbers. They use the same spacing as positive numbers, but in the opposite direction.
Negative numbers appear whenever a value falls below a chosen zero point: temperatures below freezing, debts below a balance of zero, or positions left of an origin.
Positive whole steps, negative whole steps, and zero form the integers. Integers have no fractional or decimal parts.
Whole numbers mark clean steps, but a line is not a row of separated stones. It is continuous, with space between every pair of neighboring integers.
Fractions and decimals describe positions inside those spaces. The point halfway between 0 and 1 is written as 1/2, or 0.5.
The spaces can be divided again and again. However closely the line is examined, more positions still exist between the numbers already marked.
The oldest use of numbers is counting objects: sheep, stones, fingers, marks, or anything that comes in separate units.
Counting begins at 1 and continues upward: 1, 2, 3, 4, and so on. Halves and quarters are not needed when the objects are whole.
This basic counting set has its own name in mathematics. It is called the natural numbers.
On the number line, the natural numbers are the whole steps to the right of zero: 1, 2, 3, 4, and onward.
Natural numbers work well when objects are present. A separate symbol is needed when the count has nothing in it.
Zero fills that role. It marks the absence of counted objects and also becomes the anchor point of the number line.
Adding zero to the natural numbers creates a larger set: the whole numbers.
Whole numbers are the natural counting numbers together with zero. That is the only difference between the two sets.
The number line includes the right side of zero, but it also continues to the left. That left side is where negative numbers belong.
A balance of 5 dollars is positive. A debt of 3 dollars is negative. The sign records which side of zero the value sits on.
Negative numbers are the same whole steps as positive numbers, placed to the left of zero instead of to the right.
Whole numbers and their negative versions combine to form the integers: ..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...
An integer is a clean whole step on the number line. It may be positive, negative, or zero, but it has no fractional part.
Many real quantities do not land exactly on whole steps. A length, amount, or share can fall between two integers.
Halfway between 0 and 1 is the number 1/2. It names a precise point inside the gap rather than on a whole step.
Any number that can be written as a fraction of two integers belongs to the rational numbers.
The word rational comes from ratio. A rational number is a number that can be expressed as one integer divided by another.
Rational numbers can be written as fractions, but they can also be written as decimals. The decimal form follows a clear rule.
Some rational decimals stop. For example, 1/2 is exactly 0.5, so the decimal has a final digit.
Other rational decimals repeat forever. For example, 1/3 becomes 0.333333..., with the same digit repeating without end.
A repeating decimal is still rational because it comes from a fraction and follows a predictable pattern.
A decimal is rational if it stops completely or repeats a pattern forever.
Some numbers do not fit the fraction rule. Their decimals continue forever without settling into a repeating pattern.
These decimals do not stop and do not repeat. Their digits keep going without becoming predictable.
Pi is the most famous example. Its decimal begins 3.14159265..., and it cannot be written as a simple fraction of two integers.
Numbers that cannot be written as fractions of integers are called irrational numbers.
Irrational numbers still have exact positions on the number line, even when their decimal addresses are endless.
The number line can now be built up in layers.
Integers give the clean whole-number steps across the line: negative numbers, zero, and positive numbers.
Rational numbers fill many of the gaps between those steps using fractions and decimals that stop or repeat.
Irrational numbers fill the remaining gaps with decimals that continue forever without repeating.
Together, rational and irrational numbers leave no gaps on the number line.
The complete number line is called the real numbers. Any number with a position on that line is a real number.
Mathematicians use shorthand letters for common sets of numbers instead of writing their full names every time.
Some of these letters are written in blackboard bold, such as ℕ or ℝ. The double-stroke style marks them as number sets.
The natural numbers are written as ℕ. Whole numbers are often written as W in school-level notation.
Integers are written as ℤ rather than I, because I is already used for other mathematical ideas.
The symbol ℤ comes from the German word Zahlen, meaning numbers. It represents the whole steps: negative, zero, and positive.
The rational numbers are written as ℚ.
The symbol ℚ comes from quotient. A quotient is the result of division, and rational numbers are numbers expressible as one integer divided by another.
Irrational numbers do not have a single common letter as universally familiar as ℕ, ℤ, or ℚ. They are often treated as the non-rational numbers inside the real line.
The largest set in this sequence is the real numbers, written as ℝ. It contains every number with a position on the number line.
The natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rational numbers, and irrational numbers all sit inside the real numbers.
A rule such as "double it and add three" can accept different input numbers without changing the rule itself.
If 2 goes in, 7 comes out. If 5 goes in, 13 comes out. Each input is handled in the same way.
A function is a rule that takes an allowed input and returns a definite output.
The same function can appear in words, in a table, on a graph, or as a formula.
The function is the pairing: each input is connected to its own output.
The rule "double it and add three" can be tested on several input numbers while the rule stays unchanged.
Each input-output pair becomes a point. The input gives the x-position, and the output gives the y-position.
When the points for 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 are plotted, they form an ordered pattern rather than scattered marks.
For this rule, the points fall on a straight line because the output rises by the same amount each time.
A graph places the rule on the plane, where its pattern can be seen instead of only calculated.
A ramp can rise gently or sharply. In each case, horizontal distance is paired with a change in height.
On a graph, slope measures a similar comparison: how much y changes when x changes by a chosen amount.
If x moves one step right while y rises two steps, the slope of that line is two.
Slope is more than a drawing feature. It is a rate of change built into the line.
The same structure later describes speed, growth, reaction rate, and other quantities that compare one change with another.
When time is placed on the x-axis and position on the y-axis, a graph can describe motion.
A flat line means the position is not changing, so the object is stationary during that interval.
A rising straight line means the object is moving steadily away from the starting position as time passes.
The slope of that line is the velocity, because it shows how position changes with time.
A line that describes a number rule can also describe an object changing position over time.
Slope on a graph, velocity, reaction rate, and network speed share the same mathematical structure.
Each compares a change in one quantity with a change in another quantity over the same interval.
Position per time gives velocity. Product formed per time gives reaction rate. Data per time gives bandwidth.
Mathematics gives the reusable pattern, and each science attaches that pattern to its own kind of change.
Rate is one place where different subjects use the same structure under different names.
A map has to answer two questions at once: where something is, and how to get from one place to another.
A line, a ray, and a segment each describe a different kind of straight path, but only some paths are useful for measuring real movement.
A true line extends forever in both directions. It has no fixed start and no fixed end, so it cannot describe a finished movement.
A ray has a starting point and a direction. It can point the right way, but it does not say where the movement stops.
A useful movement needs a start, a direction, and a finish. That is why the next object has to carry more information than a plain line or ray.
A line segment has a start and an end. Because both endpoints are fixed, its length can be measured.
A segment can represent a distance such as 10 meters, because it is trapped between two points instead of running forever.
A plain segment still has a weakness: it shows length, but it does not mark which endpoint is the beginning and which is the destination.
Length alone is a scalar. A vector needs both size and direction, so the segment must be given an orientation.
A vector arrow is a line segment with direction added. The tail marks the starting point, and the arrowhead marks the direction of travel.
The length of the arrow represents magnitude. A longer arrow represents a larger speed, force, displacement, or other vector quantity.
In mathematics, this object is often called a directed line segment. In physics, it is usually called a vector arrow.
The vector arrow carries two pieces of information at once: how much, and which way.
Vector arrows are used whenever size and direction matter together.
A car moving 30 miles per hour east can be drawn as an arrow pointing east, with length representing the speed.
If the speed increases to 60 miles per hour east, the arrow points the same way but becomes longer.
The drawing turns motion into geometry. Direction is shown by the arrowhead, and magnitude is shown by the arrow's length.
Scalars add by size alone. One kilogram plus one kilogram is always two kilograms because direction is not involved.
Vectors cannot be added by size alone. One meter north followed by one meter south returns to the starting point.
In vector addition, equal sizes can combine to make zero, double, or something in between, depending on their directions.
Direction changes the result. Vector addition must combine both the lengths and the directions of the arrows.
A movement of 3 meters east followed by 4 meters north can be drawn as two arrows placed head-to-tail.
The first arrow ends where the second arrow begins, creating a path with one starting point and one final point.
A single arrow can be drawn directly from the starting point to the final point.
That single arrow is the resultant vector. It represents the combined effect of the two original movements.
A drawn arrow is useful on paper, but calculation needs numbers.
A vector can be written as a list of components, with each component measuring movement along one axis.
A movement of 3 steps east and 4 steps north can be written as [3, 4].
The arrow and the list describe the same vector in different forms: one visual, one numerical.
A two-component vector describes movement on a flat plane.
A three-component vector describes movement in physical space, using directions such as east, north, and up.
The same idea can continue beyond three components. A vector can have four, ten, or thousands of numbers.
High-dimensional vectors cannot be pictured easily, but they can still be calculated. The mathematics does not require the space to be drawable.
A vector can describe more than physical position. It can also store measurements about an object, signal, image, or pattern.
A three-number vector can describe a location in space. A longer vector can describe features such as distances, colors, intensities, or proportions.
In machine learning, data is often represented as points in high-dimensional coordinate spaces.
Comparing two data points can become a geometry problem: measure how close their vectors are in that space.
Slope measures steepness. In an equation such as y = 2x, the line rises two steps for every one step across.
Steepness is not enough to locate the line. Many different lines can have the same slope but sit at different heights.
To fix the line in place, the equation also needs the height where the line crosses the y-axis.
In y = 2x + 3, the slope is still 2, but the whole line is shifted upward so it crosses the y-axis at 3.
The equation y = mx + c describes a straight line using two controlling numbers.
The number m controls the slope: how steeply the line rises or falls.
Changing m rotates the line, making it steeper, flatter, rising, or falling.
The number c controls the y-intercept: the height where the line crosses the vertical axis.
A line stretches forever, but its position is fixed by these two features: slope and intercept.
Once a line is described by slope and intercept, some relationships can be seen without drawing the graph.
The equations y = 2x + 3 and y = 2x - 4 have different intercepts but the same slope.
One line crosses the y-axis at 3, and the other crosses at -4. Both have slope 2.
Because the slopes match, the two lines rise at the same angle and never meet. They are parallel.
Equal slopes mean equal steepness. Different intercepts place the lines at different heights.
The distance between two points is easy to measure when they sit on the same horizontal or vertical grid line.
When two points are separated diagonally, horizontal or vertical counting alone no longer gives the full distance.
The diagonal gap can be treated as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle built from horizontal and vertical changes.
Pythagoras' theorem combines the horizontal change and vertical change to calculate the diagonal distance.
This is the same structure used in digital maps: two coordinate positions create a triangle, and the diagonal gives the distance between them.
A drawn shape can be slightly crooked, but coordinates remove the guesswork. Every important point is given an exact numerical address.
Once points have coordinates, geometry can be checked by calculation instead of by eye. A diagram becomes data.
The number line gives one coordinate for position on a line. The coordinate plane gives two coordinates for position on a surface.
This is the shift coordinate geometry makes: shapes are still visual, but their properties can now be measured with arithmetic.
The aim is no longer only to draw lines and shapes. The aim is to prove what they are using numbers.
The coordinate plane is built from two number lines crossing at zero: a horizontal x-axis and a vertical y-axis.
Their crossing point is the origin, written as (0, 0). Every other point is measured relative to that point.
A point is written as an ordered pair, (x, y). The first number gives horizontal position; the second gives vertical position.
The order matters. The points (3, 4) and (4, 3) usually land in different places because the coordinates have different roles.
The axes divide the plane into four quadrants, giving a simple map for positive and negative x and y positions.
To plot a point such as (3, 4), move 3 units along the x-direction and then 4 units in the y-direction.
Negative coordinates move in the opposite direction: negative x moves left, and negative y moves downward.
Reading a point reverses the process. Its horizontal position gives x, and its vertical position gives y.
Plotting turns numbers into a position. Reading turns a position back into numbers.
This two-way translation is the basic move of coordinate geometry: number pair to point, point back to number pair.

boards.title: A line is a set of points

tags.subject: maths
tags.concept: A line is a set of points

floors.content: In coordinate geometry, a line is not only a stroke on a diagram. It is a set of points that obey the same rule.
A vertical line keeps x fixed while y changes. For example, every point on x = 3 has horizontal position 3.
A horizontal line keeps y fixed while x changes. For example, every point on y = 2 has vertical position 2.
Slanted lines also follow rules, but both coordinates change together instead of one coordinate staying fixed.
The central question becomes: what rule connects x and y for all points on this line?

boards.title: A slanted line has a rule

tags.subject: maths
tags.concept: A slanted line has a rule

floors.content: A slanted line can be recognized by a steady relationship between x and y.
On the line y = 2x, every y-value is double its x-value: (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6), and so on.
The equation is not a label added afterward. It is the rule that decides which points belong on the line.
Changing the multiplier changes the steepness. The line y = 3x rises faster than y = 2x.
The multiplier describes how much y changes for each one-unit change in x. That number is the slope.
Slope measures the rate at which y changes compared with x along a straight line.
Between two points, the vertical change is Δy and the horizontal change is Δx.
The slope is written as m = Δy / Δx, or m = (y₂ - y₁) / (x₂ - x₁).
For the points (1, 2) and (4, 8), Δy = 6 and Δx = 3, so the slope is 2.
A straight line has the same slope between any two points on it. That constant slope is what makes it straight.
Most non-vertical straight lines can be written in the form y = mx + c.
The number m is the slope. It controls how steeply the line rises or falls.
The number c is the y-intercept. It tells where the line crosses the y-axis.
In y = 2x + 3, the slope is 2 and the y-intercept is 3.
Two numbers, m and c, fix the whole line: its steepness and its vertical position.

boards.title: Building a line from two points

tags.subject: maths
tags.concept: Building a line from two points

floors.content: Two distinct points determine exactly one straight line.
Given two points, first find the slope using m = (y₂ - y₁) / (x₂ - x₁).
Then place one point and the slope into y = mx + c to solve for c.
For (2, 7) and (5, 16), the slope is 3. Substituting (2, 7) gives c = 1.
The line through those points is y = 3x + 1. The equation can now generate every point on the line.
Parallel lines have the same slope. They rise or fall at the same rate.
The lines y = 2x + 3 and y = 2x - 4 both have slope 2.
Their y-intercepts differ, so they sit at different heights, but their steepness is identical.
Because the slopes match, the distance between the lines never closes. They do not meet.
Equal slopes prove parallel lines, as long as the intercepts are different.
Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle.
For two non-vertical lines, perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals.
A line with slope 2 is perpendicular to a line with slope -1/2.
The test is m₁ × m₂ = -1. If the product of the slopes is -1, the lines meet at 90°.
Horizontal and vertical lines are also perpendicular, though the slope formula treats vertical lines as a special case.
The distance between two points on a grid can be found by building a right-angled triangle between them.
The horizontal difference gives Δx. The vertical difference gives Δy.
The straight-line distance is the hypotenuse, so Pythagoras gives d = √(Δx² + Δy²).
The distance formula is Pythagoras written for coordinates.
The midpoint is the point exactly halfway between two given points.
On a line, the midpoint is found by averaging the two positions. On a grid, the same idea is applied twice.
Average the x-values to get the midpoint's x-coordinate. Average the y-values to get its y-coordinate.
Distance gives a segment's length. Midpoint gives its center.
A polygon on a coordinate grid can be described by listing its vertices in order.
Three vertices form a triangle. Four vertices form a quadrilateral, depending on how the points are arranged.
Once the vertices are known, the side lengths and slopes can be calculated.
That means the shape's properties are not guessed from the drawing. They are checked from the coordinates.
A coordinate shape is a visual figure with a numerical description underneath it.
Coordinates allow a shape to be proved rather than judged by appearance.
Side lengths can be checked using the distance formula.
Parallel and perpendicular sides can be checked using slopes.
A quadrilateral with opposite sides equal and a right angle can be confirmed as a rectangle.
Coordinate geometry turns visual claims into arithmetic checks.
A point on the plane is written as (x, y), with x giving horizontal position and y giving vertical position.
A line is a set of points satisfying a rule. Non-vertical lines can often be written as y = mx + c.
Slope is m = Δy / Δx. It measures how much y changes for each change in x.
Parallel lines have equal slopes. Perpendicular non-vertical lines have slopes whose product is -1.
Distance, midpoint, slope, and equations let coordinates prove facts about lines and shapes.
A function can be pictured as a simple machine: an input goes in, a fixed process happens, and an output comes out.
A vending machine makes the structure visible. A code such as A1 is the input, and the item that drops out is the output.
The useful part is the fixed connection between the code and the item, not the metal box itself.
A function is a rule that assigns each allowed input exactly one output.
This makes functions a way to describe relationships between quantities rather than isolated numbers.
The core condition is strict: one input cannot produce two different outputs.
If A1 gives cola in a vending machine, A1 should give cola whenever the same machine is set the same way.
Different inputs may still share one output. A1 and B4 could both be assigned to the same drink.
That is allowed because each input still has one assigned result. The problem appears only when one input points to more than one output.
A function may be many-to-one, but it cannot be one-to-many.
Function notation gives a compact way to name a relationship and show which input is being used.
The input is often called x. The function itself is often named f.
The expression f(x) is read as "f of x." It means the output produced when x is placed into f.
If the function doubles the input, it can be written as f(x) = 2x.
Then f(5) means f acts on 5, giving f(5) = 10.
A function does not always accept every possible input.
The set of inputs a function is allowed to use is called its domain.
A function also has a set of outputs it can actually produce.
The set of possible outputs is called the range.
Domain describes what can go in. Range describes what can come out.
A function can be shown on a coordinate graph by plotting input-output pairs.
The input usually becomes the x-coordinate, and the output becomes the y-coordinate.
The one-output condition creates a visual test: each x-value should match at most one y-value.
A vertical line crossing the graph should not hit the curve in more than one place.
If one vertical line touches the graph twice, one input has two outputs, so the graph does not represent a function.
A linear function changes by a constant amount for each equal step in the input.
If the function is f(x) = x + 2, then increasing x by 1 also increases the output by 1.
When plotted, this steady change forms a straight line.
A constant speed is a physical example: each extra hour adds the same distance.
Linear functions are the function form of constant rate.
An exponential function grows or shrinks by multiplying rather than adding.
A doubling pattern goes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, with each output becoming the base for the next step.
In an exponential function such as f(x) = 2^x, the input appears in the exponent.
On a graph, exponential growth may begin slowly and then rise very quickly as the input increases.
Compound interest, population growth, radioactive decay, and repeated doubling all use exponential patterns.
A quadratic function contains a squared input, such as x^2.
Squaring makes the output change faster as the input moves farther from zero.
The graph of a simple quadratic function is a parabola.
A parabola is a symmetric U-shaped curve, opening upward or downward depending on the equation.
Projectile paths, area formulas, and many optimization problems can be modeled with quadratic functions.
An inverse function reverses the action of another function.
If a function sends an input to an output, its inverse sends that output back to the original input.
This only works cleanly when each output came from one unique input.
If two different inputs share the same output, the reverse direction becomes ambiguous.
For this reason, inverse functions depend on one-to-one relationships.
Complex processes often happen as chains of smaller functions.
In a composite function, the output of one function becomes the input of another.
The notation f(g(x)) means g acts on x first, then f acts on the result.
This allows simple functions to be combined into larger functions without losing the input-output structure.
Software models, simulations, and multi-step calculations often rely on functions feeding outputs into other functions.

boards.title: A line has a constant change

tags.subject: maths
tags.concept: A line has a constant change

floors.content: On a coordinate grid, a straight line is a set of points connected by one steady relationship between x and y.
The important feature is consistency. Each equal step in x produces the same change in y.
That steady change is what separates a straight line from a curve, where the rate of change may vary from point to point.
Lines and gradients begin with this fact: a straight line changes at a constant rate.
Gradient measures how steeply a line rises or falls as it moves across the grid.
It compares vertical change with horizontal change: how much y changes for a chosen change in x.
The common formula is gradient = rise / run, or m = Δy / Δx.
A larger gradient means the line changes more sharply. A smaller gradient means the line changes more gently.
Gradient turns the visual idea of steepness into a number that can be calculated.
To find a gradient, choose two points on the line and compare their coordinates.
The rise is the vertical change between the points. The run is the horizontal change between the same two points.
For points (1, 2) and (4, 8), the rise is 6 and the run is 3.
The gradient is 6 / 3 = 2, so the line rises 2 units for every 1 unit across.
On a straight line, any two points give the same gradient because the rate of change is constant.
The sign of the gradient gives the line's direction.
A positive gradient means the line rises from left to right.
A negative gradient means the line falls from left to right.
A gradient of 2 rises 2 units for every 1 unit across. A gradient of -2 falls 2 units for every 1 unit across.
The size of the gradient gives steepness, while the sign gives direction.
A horizontal line has no vertical change as x changes.
Since the rise is zero, every horizontal line has gradient 0.
A vertical line has no horizontal change as y changes.
Since the run is zero, the gradient calculation would require division by zero.
For that reason, a vertical line has undefined gradient rather than gradient 0.
Gradient gives steepness and direction, but it does not fix the line's exact position.
Many lines can share the same gradient while crossing the grid at different heights.
The y-intercept is the point where the line crosses the y-axis.
At the y-axis, x = 0. The y-intercept is therefore the value of y when x is 0.
The intercept anchors the line vertically while the gradient controls its tilt.
The equation y = mx + c stores the two key features of a non-vertical straight line.
The m gives the gradient: the rate at which y changes as x changes.
The c gives the y-intercept: the height where the line crosses the y-axis.
In y = 2x + 3, the gradient is 2 and the y-intercept is 3.
Changing m changes the tilt. Changing c shifts the line up or down without changing its tilt.
Lines with the same gradient rise or fall at the same rate.
If their intercepts are different, they sit at different heights but keep the same direction.
Such lines are parallel because the gap between them never closes.
The equations y = 2x + 3 and y = 2x - 4 are parallel because both have gradient 2.
Matching gradients are enough to prove that two non-identical straight lines are parallel.

boards.title: Finding a line from two points

tags.subject: maths
tags.concept: Finding a line from two points

floors.content: Two points are enough to determine one straight line.
First, use the two points to calculate the gradient with m = Δy / Δx.
Then substitute one point into y = mx + c to find the intercept.
Once m and c are known, the equation describes the whole line.
This converts a pair of plotted points into an algebraic rule.
Gradient is not only a property of drawn lines. It is a way to describe constant change.
Speed is change in position over time. Gradient is change in y over change in x.
This is why distance-time graphs, cost graphs, growth graphs, and many scientific graphs use gradients.
A straight line means the rate stays constant. A steeper line means the rate is larger.
Lines and gradients prepare the ground for rates, motion graphs, and eventually calculus.
An exponent is a compact way to write repeated multiplication, where the base is reused as a factor a specific number of times.
For example, 2^4 means 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2. The base is 2, and the exponent is 4.
The notation matters because multiplication chains become difficult to read once the number of repeated factors grows beyond a few terms.
Exponents keep the structure visible. They show both the repeated number and the length of the repetition in one expression.
Once exponents are read this way, the laws of exponents become patterns in multiplication rather than separate facts to memorize.
When two powers have the same base, multiplying them joins their repeated multiplication chains into one longer chain of matching factors.
The expression 3^2 \times 3^4 means two factors of 3 followed by four more factors of 3 in the same product.
Altogether, there are six factors of 3, so the product is 3^6 rather than a new kind of operation.
This is why the exponent law says a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n} when the base is the same.
The base does not change. Only the count of repeated factors changes, because the two multiplication chains have been joined together.
A negative exponent does not make the final value negative. It changes the position of the power inside a fraction.
For example, 2^{-3} means \frac{1}{2^3}, which equals \frac{1}{8} after the power in the denominator is evaluated.
This extends the ordinary exponent pattern below zero, where each step downward divides by the base again instead of multiplying.
Positive exponents move upward by repeated multiplication. Negative exponents move the same pattern downward by repeated division through reciprocal powers.
Negative exponents are therefore a compact notation for reciprocal powers, especially when very small quantities need to be written cleanly.
Fractional exponents connect powers and roots, so roots become part of the same notation rather than a separate mathematical language.
The denominator of the exponent tells which root is being taken. For example, x^{1/2} means \sqrt{x}, the square root.
Similarly, x^{1/3} means the cube root of x, because cubing reverses the cube-root operation and returns to x.
More generally, x^{1/n} means the number that must be raised to the power n to produce x again.
This notation lets powers and roots combine smoothly, which becomes important in algebra, graphs, physics, and rate formulas involving change.
Linear growth adds the same amount each step, while exponential growth multiplies by the same factor at every step instead.
A doubling pattern goes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Each amount is multiplied by 2 to produce the next amount.
The early values can look small, but repeated multiplication compounds quickly because each new value becomes the base for the next step.
That is why exponential graphs can appear almost flat at first, then rise sharply once the multiplied values become large.
Compound interest, population growth, viral spread, and chain reactions all use this structure of repeated multiplication over time and scale.

boards.title: Exponential decay shrinks by a factor

tags.subject: maths
tags.concept: Exponential decay shrinks by a factor

floors.content: Exponential decay is the same structure as exponential growth, but each step keeps only a fixed fraction of the previous amount.
If a quantity halves each hour, 80 becomes 40, then 20, then 10, with the same factor applied each time.
The amount does not fall by equal subtraction. It falls by equal proportion, which makes the decrease smaller as the quantity shrinks.
This is why decay curves drop quickly at first, then flatten as there is less remaining quantity to lose at later stages.
Radioactive decay, cooling, capacitor discharge, and medicine leaving the bloodstream can all be modeled with exponential decay over time and quantity.
A logarithm reverses the question asked by an exponent. It asks which power was needed to produce a given number.
If 10^3 = 1000, then \log_{10}(1000) = 3, because 3 is the exponent that produces 1000 from base 10.
The base of the logarithm tells which number was being powered. The answer is the exponent attached to that base.
Logarithms are not a new kind of arithmetic. They are a way of reading exponential statements from the other direction.
This makes logarithms useful whenever an unknown value is sitting in the exponent instead of beside the base in an equation.
Logarithms connect multiplication and addition because multiplying powers with the same base adds their exponents rather than multiplying them directly.
This is the reason \log(ab) = \log(a) + \log(b), as long as the logarithms use the same base throughout.
The logarithm is reading the exponent hidden behind each number, so multiplying the numbers becomes adding those hidden exponents instead.
This property made logarithms powerful calculation tools long before electronic calculators, because hard multiplication could be converted into easier addition.
The same idea still matters in algebra, data scales, signal measurement, and any situation where multiplicative change needs to be compared.
The number e appears when growth is compounded continuously, meaning the compounding is treated as happening without separate time jumps.
Its decimal begins near 2.718, but the exact decimal is less important than the continuous-change behavior it represents in formulas.
The function e^x is special because its rate of change matches its own value at every point on the graph.
That property makes e central in calculus, especially when describing growth, decay, cooling, charging, and many physical systems mathematically over time.
In this sense, e is not chosen for convenience. It appears naturally when change depends on the current amount present.
Exponential functions and logarithmic functions undo each other, so each one reverses the action of the other in equations and graphs.
If an exponential function sends 3 to 1000, the matching logarithm sends 1000 back to 3 again as its exponent.
On a coordinate graph, inverse functions mirror each other across the line y = x, swapping inputs and outputs between axes.
This inverse relationship is what allows logarithms to solve equations where the unknown value appears in the exponent instead of the base.
Exponents describe repeated multiplication moving forward. Logarithms recover the exponent that created the result from a chosen base in reverse.

boards.title: A matrix is a rectangular array

tags.subject: maths
tags.concept: A matrix is a rectangular array

floors.content: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, symbols, or expressions arranged in rows and columns as one mathematical object.
It may look like a small table, but in mathematics the arrangement is part of the object itself, not decoration.
Each position in the array matters. Moving a number to a different row or column can change the matrix and its meaning.
A spreadsheet can help with the first visual idea, but a matrix is not defined by software, labels, or cells.
The useful definition is this: a matrix is one structured object whose entries are organized by row and column position.
Each value inside a matrix is called an entry, and every entry has a position determined by its row and column.
Mathematicians usually name entries with indices. The notation a_{3,2} means the entry in row 3, column 2 of matrix A.
The row number is written first, then the column number. This order is part of the notation and should not be swapped.
Row 2, column 3 and row 3, column 2 are different positions, even if the same number appears in both places.
Once the address system is clear, a matrix becomes organized information rather than a block of disconnected symbols on a page.

boards.title: Matrix size is rows by columns

tags.subject: maths
tags.concept: Matrix size is rows by columns

floors.content: The size of a matrix is given by its number of rows followed by its number of columns, in that order.
A matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns is called a 2 \times 3 matrix, read as two by three.
A 3 \times 2 matrix also contains six entries, but it has a different shape and therefore behaves differently in operations.
Matrix dimensions are not decoration. They decide which operations are possible and how the result of an operation will be shaped.
This is why matrices with the same number of entries can still be different mathematical objects with different uses and meanings.
Two matrices can be added only when they have the same dimensions: the same number of rows and the same number of columns.
Addition is done entry by entry. The entry in row 1, column 1 adds to the entry in row 1, column 1.
The same pairing continues across the entire matrix, so every position in the first matrix matches one position in the second.
If the dimensions do not match, there is no complete row-column pairing, so matrix addition is not defined for those matrices.
The operation respects structure. Matrices add cleanly only when their shapes line up exactly from the first entry to the last.
A matrix can represent data whenever information can be arranged in rows and columns with consistent meaning across the whole array.
A black-and-white image, for example, can be represented as a matrix where each entry records the brightness of one pixel.
A value such as 0 may represent black, 255 may represent white, and values between them represent grey levels of brightness.
The matrix is not the picture itself. It is a numerical representation that a computer can store, process, and transform.
This is one reason matrices appear in imaging, statistics, maps, networks, scientific measurement, engineering, economics, and numerical computation across many fields.
A matrix can also represent a transformation, meaning a systematic action that sends points or vectors to new positions in space.
For example, the matrix \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} doubles the x-coordinate and leaves the y-coordinate unchanged.
Under that transformation, the point (3,4) becomes (6,4) because the horizontal coordinate is stretched by a factor of 2.
In this setting, the entries of the matrix describe how space is stretched, compressed, reflected, rotated, or sheared by the transformation.
This gives matrices a second major role: they can store data, but they can also describe actions on data or space.

boards.title: The identity matrix leaves objects unchanged

tags.subject: maths
tags.concept: The identity matrix leaves objects unchanged

floors.content: The identity matrix is the matrix version of doing nothing to a vector or point during a transformation in space.
In two dimensions, the identity matrix is \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}, and it sends (x,y) back to (x,y).
It plays a role similar to the number 1 in multiplication, because applying it leaves the object unchanged after the operation.
The identity matrix matters because transformations need a clear baseline: the transformation that changes nothing at all to the object.
Once matrices are treated as transformations, the identity matrix becomes the neutral element among those transformations under matrix multiplication in algebra.

boards.title: Rotation can be written as a matrix

tags.subject: maths
tags.concept: Rotation can be written as a matrix

floors.content: A rotation matrix represents a turn around the origin using entries arranged in a specific pattern inside the matrix itself.
A 90^\circ counterclockwise rotation sends (1,0) to (0,1) and is represented by \begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
More general rotation matrices use sine and cosine because those functions describe circular movement around the origin at different angles.
This is where trigonometry and matrices connect: trigonometry describes the turn, and the matrix applies it consistently to every point.
The spreadsheet comparison is only the entrance. A matrix begins as an array, then becomes a language for data and transformation.
Right triangles give a useful starting point for trigonometry, but they only handle acute angles inside a triangle with fixed sides.
The unit circle extends the same ideas to every angle by placing a circle of radius 1 around the origin.
An angle \theta is measured from the positive x-axis to a radius ending at a point on the circle.
The x-coordinate of that point is \cos\theta, and the y-coordinate is \sin\theta for that angle on the circle.
With this definition, sine and cosine can describe turning, rotation, waves, and repeating motion beyond right-triangle geometry alone in many contexts.
The exact values for 30^\circ, 45^\circ, and 60^\circ come from two standard triangles, not from isolated table entries.
Cutting a square along its diagonal creates a 45^\circ-45^\circ-90^\circ triangle with two equal shorter sides.
That equality explains why \sin45^\circ and \cos45^\circ have the same value on the unit circle and in right triangles.
Cutting an equilateral triangle in half creates a 30^\circ-60^\circ-90^\circ triangle with side ratio 1:\sqrt{3}:2.
These two triangles generate the familiar exact values, so the table becomes a summary of geometry rather than memorized data.
Trigonometry has a small set of exact reference values for sine, cosine, and tangent at common angles used repeatedly in problems.
The usual reference angles are 0^\circ, 30^\circ, 45^\circ, 60^\circ, and 90^\circ, measured from the positive x-axis.
Along these angles, sine rises from 0 to 1, while cosine follows the same pattern in reverse order across the table.
Tangent is defined by \tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} wherever \cos\theta is not zero, so division is valid.
Exact values such as \frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, and \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} keep the geometry visible.
As a point moves around the unit circle, its vertical coordinate rises, falls, and returns to the same height after one turn.
Plotting that vertical coordinate against the angle produces the sine wave, one of the basic periodic graphs in mathematics and physics.
Cosine comes from the horizontal coordinate, so it follows the same repeating pattern with a different starting position on the graph.
Both graphs have amplitude 1, midline 0, and period 2\pi, meaning they repeat after one full turn around the circle.
Sound, tides, alternating current, pendulum motion, and circular motion all connect to trigonometry through repeating change over time and space.
Tangent behaves differently from sine and cosine because it is not limited to values between -1 and 1 on its graph.
Since \tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}, tangent grows very large when \cos\theta gets close to zero in the denominator.
On its graph, tangent has vertical asymptotes where the function is undefined because division by zero would occur there at those angles.
Tangent also measures slope: a line making angle \theta with the positive x-axis has slope \tan\theta in coordinate geometry.
This links trigonometry to gradients, direction, and steepness, not only to side lengths inside triangles or values on circles alone.

boards.title: Radians measure angle by arc length

tags.subject: maths
tags.concept: Radians measure angle by arc length

floors.content: Degrees are useful for everyday angle measurement, but radians are built from the geometry of the circle itself and its arc lengths.
One radian is the angle formed when the arc length on a circle is equal to the radius of that circle.
A full turn is 2\pi radians, half a turn is \pi radians, and a quarter turn is \frac{\pi}{2} radians.
Radians make circular formulas cleaner because arc length becomes s=r\theta when \theta is measured in radians rather than degrees.
They also make calculus with sine and cosine work naturally, without extra conversion factors attached to the derivatives of these functions.
A function gives outputs from inputs, but calculus often asks what happens as the input moves toward a chosen value.
A limit describes the value a function approaches as the input gets closer and closer to a point from nearby inputs.
The point being approached does not need to be reached for the nearby behavior of the function to become clear.
This is the first bridge from functions to calculus: studying motion toward a value rather than only evaluating at the value.
Limits make it possible to talk precisely about trends, gaps, curves, rates, and change near a point on a function.

boards.title: Nearby values can reveal a pattern

tags.subject: maths
tags.concept: Nearby values can reveal a pattern

floors.content: A limit is usually found by looking at function values close to the input being studied, rather than only at the input itself.
If values from the left and right both move toward the same output, the function has a limit there at that point.
The actual value of the function at the point may agree with the limit, differ from it, or be undefined.
This separates local behavior from direct substitution, which is why limits are useful when formulas have gaps or undefined points.
The important question is not only what the function equals, but what the function is approaching nearby from both sides.
A two-sided limit exists only when the function approaches the same value from both directions around the input being studied.
The left-hand limit studies inputs smaller than the point, while the right-hand limit studies inputs larger than the point being approached.
If both sides approach the same output, the two-sided limit exists and equals that shared value at the point itself.
If the left and right sides approach different values, the function has no single limit at that point on the graph.
This matters because calculus depends on stable local behavior, not on two directions giving conflicting answers near the same input.
A hole occurs when the nearby values approach one output, but the function is missing or defined differently at the point.
In that case, the limit can still exist because the surrounding behavior points toward one clear value from both sides.
A jump occurs when the function approaches one value from the left and another value from the right at the same input.
A jump has no two-sided limit at the jump point because the two approaches disagree with each other there completely.
Limits therefore distinguish between removable breaks, where the nearby pattern is stable, and jumps, where the pattern splits into two sides.
Some formulas cannot be evaluated directly at a point because substitution creates an expression such as division by zero in the formula.
A limit asks whether the formula still approaches a stable value as the input gets close to that point from nearby values.
Algebra can sometimes simplify the expression and reveal the value that the nearby points were approaching all along in the pattern.
This does not pretend the forbidden input is allowed. It studies the behavior around the forbidden input instead, using nearby values.
That distinction is essential for calculus, where meaningful patterns often appear at points that direct substitution cannot handle cleanly by itself.
Some limits study what happens as the input grows without bound instead of approaching a fixed number on the number line.
A function may approach a horizontal level as x becomes very large or very negative over the long run in the graph.
That horizontal level is called a horizontal asymptote when the graph gets closer to it over the long run without necessarily touching it.
Other functions grow without bound, meaning their outputs become larger and larger instead of settling near a finite value at all.
Limits at infinity describe long-term behavior, which is useful in graphs, models, sequences, and rates of decay over time and change.

boards.title: Continuity means no break in the limit

tags.subject: maths
tags.concept: Continuity means no break in the limit

floors.content: A function is continuous at a point when its value and its limit at that point agree exactly with each other.
That means the function is defined there, the nearby values approach a limit, and the limit equals the function value.
On a graph, continuity means the curve passes through the point without a hole, jump, or break in its path.
Continuity is not only a visual idea. It is a statement about the agreement between value and approach at a point.
This prepares the ground for differentiation, because derivatives require stable behavior near the point being studied on the curve itself.
The second bridge to differentiation begins when a limit is used to study change over smaller and smaller intervals around a point.
A secant slope measures average change between two points on a curve by comparing vertical change with horizontal change between them.
As the two points move closer together, the secant slope may approach one stable value at the chosen point on the curve.
That limiting value is the slope of the tangent line at the point, if the limit exists there for the curve.
Differentiation begins here: the derivative is a limit of average rates of change as the interval shrinks to zero at the point.
A straight line has one slope everywhere, but a curve changes its steepness from point to point along its path.
Differentiation finds the slope of a curve at one chosen point by studying slopes over shrinking intervals around that point.
The average slope between two nearby points is called a secant slope, because the line cuts through the curve between them.
As the second point moves closer to the first, those secant slopes may approach one stable value for the curve.
That limiting value is the derivative, which gives the slope of the tangent line at that point on the curve.

boards.title: The derivative is a limit of change

tags.subject: maths
tags.concept: The derivative is a limit of change

floors.content: The derivative of a function records how fast the output changes compared with the input at a specific point locally.
In symbols, the derivative can be written as f'(x) or as \frac{dy}{dx} when y=f(x) for the same idea.
The notation \frac{dy}{dx} compares a small change in y with a small change in x near a point.
The derivative becomes exact when that comparison is taken as a limit while the change in x shrinks toward zero.
This is why differentiation belongs after limits: it is built from the limit of shrinking average rates of change near a point.
The function y=x^2 gives a clean first example because its slope changes smoothly from point to point along the curve.
Near x=3, the slopes between nearby points on the curve get closer and closer to 6 as the interval shrinks.
This means the tangent line to y=x^2 at x=3 has slope 6 at that exact point, not across an interval.
More generally, the derivative of x^2 is 2x, so the local slope depends on the chosen input value on the graph.
Differentiation turns a function into another function that reports the original function's rate of change at each input value in its domain.

boards.title: The power rule is a shortcut

tags.subject: maths
tags.concept: The power rule is a shortcut

floors.content: Once the derivative pattern is known, many derivatives do not need to be rebuilt from the limit definition each time.
The power rule says that for x^n, the exponent moves in front and the exponent is reduced by one.
In notation, \frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1} for powers where the rule applies in elementary differentiation and algebra.
For example, the derivative of x^4 is 4x^3, and the derivative of 5x^4 is 20x^3 by the power rule.
Constants by themselves have derivative 0 because a horizontal line has no change in height as x changes at all.
The derivative of a product is not usually the product of the derivatives, because both factors may change together at once.
The product rule accounts for both contributions: one factor changes while the other is held, then the roles switch between factors.
In notation, (fg)'=f'g+fg', where each term captures one part of the product's changing behavior in the calculation of change.
Division has its own pattern, called the quotient rule, because the numerator and denominator affect the fraction differently as they change.
These rules matter whenever changing quantities multiply or divide, including area, revenue, density, ratios, and physical formulas in applications like these.
Many functions are built in layers, where one function acts first and another function acts on its output afterward inside the composition.
The chain rule differentiates the outside layer, then multiplies by the derivative of the inside layer underneath in the composition.
For (3x^2+5)^7, the outside contributes 7(3x^2+5)^6, and the inside contributes 6x from differentiating 3x^2+5.
Multiplying those parts gives the derivative 42x(3x^2+5)^6 for the full layered expression after simplification of the product.
The chain rule matters because layered functions appear in physics, geometry, statistics, optimization, computer-based models, and simulations of real systems.
Derivatives are not only geometric slopes. They also describe rates of change in quantities that vary over time or space.
Velocity is the derivative of position because it measures how quickly position changes with respect to time or another time unit.
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity because it measures how quickly velocity itself changes over time during motion along a path.
Similar rate ideas appear in temperature change, medicine concentration, current flow, population change, and energy transfer in physical systems over time.
In each case, differentiation gives a precise language for how fast one quantity is changing relative to another quantity in context.
A derivative can show where a function is increasing, decreasing, or flattening out across a chosen interval on the graph itself.
When the derivative is positive, the function is rising. When the derivative is negative, the function is falling on that interval.
Points where the derivative equals zero can mark local maxima, local minima, or flat points that are neither in context.
Optimization uses this information to find best values, such as maximum height, minimum cost, or most efficient design for a problem.
This makes differentiation a tool for studying change, motion, and decisions, not only for finding slopes on graphs alone in isolation.
